# 0.15.156

**Nobody can ask to control your computer any more. You invite them.**

Derek, 7 October 2026: *"i think its actually better to frame it like inviting to control during a
call rather than ask to control"* — and *"make sure consent starts with the person at risk and that
this is reflected by all UI"*.

It does now, and not only in the wording. The question that used to appear on your screen —
*"X wants to control this computer"* — has not been made harder to raise. It has been **removed**.
There is no signal that produces it and no command that sends one. An offer that was never made
cannot be answered at all, which is a stronger thing than a question that is dropped.

## How it works now

Three acts, and two of them are yours.

1. **You invite.** While you are sharing a screen, your own call bar has a button. It opens a sheet
   that says what they will be able to do, what it is **not** — not your other screens, not your
   files, nothing that asks for administrator rights, never the lock screen — and the key that ends
   it. With more than one person in the call you pick who first.
2. **They take it up.** Their side is short and says one thing that matters: you are watching, and
   you can take it back whenever you like. No list of consequences, because they are not the one at
   risk.
3. **Your machine opens the door.** There is no second prompt here. You consented at the sheet,
   before anybody had been offered anything; asking you the same question again at the moment it
   matters is how people learn to click through it.

The offer is **withdrawable right up to the last moment**, lapses on its own after two minutes if
they never answer, is spent by one answer, and cannot outlive the share or the call. While it runs,
the red bar is still there, still undismissable, still naming the key — and only a real press of
that key counts.

## The one thing somebody watching can do

They can say **"I'd like to be given it."** That is all. It cannot prompt you, make a sound, or put
anything on your screen that has to be dismissed. It becomes a small mark on your own button and a
line in your own picker, found when you go looking, and never before.

Whether their asking reaches you at all is a door, per person, **shut by default**. The rung in
Access used to read *"Ask for control"* and its guard sheet said it granted the right to ask. It now
reads **"Ask to be given control"** and says what is true: nobody can ask for control; this only
lets them say they would like it.

## Two things found while doing it

- **The share's switch was quietly opening a permission for everyone in the call.** Ticking "Allow
  them to ask for control" also called `door_set(control, open)` on every person in the call,
  without saying so. That was defensible when the door meant *may ask* and the switch was how you
  let them. In the new direction the door means close to the opposite, so the application would have
  been granting a standing permission on your behalf — the one move this whole flow exists to
  prevent. The switch now touches nothing but itself, and is called **"Can be handed control"**.
- **A second stylesheet rule was re-breaking the red bar.** `width: max-content` on `.rc-bar`, added
  for a floating bar that no longer exists, was overriding the real banner's full-width rule — the
  shrink-to-fit bug that once put the Stop button outside its own box, back again from a different
  direction. Deleted. The walk now measures that the bar spans the window and that a click where
  Stop is painted actually lands on Stop.

## What was already there, and what this changed

Almost none of the machinery is new. The pointer lock, the batched input, the undismissable banner,
the stop key read below the application, the device pinning, the round-trip measurement and the
native injection have all been in the build. What was wrong was the **direction**, and one file that
had grown a second, parallel signalling path of its own — so its gates were drawn rather than
enforced. There is one path now, and it is the core's.

## Verified

- `test/e2e-control.mjs` was rewritten for the new direction and walks all nine frames on two real
  devices: 31 assertions, none failing. It writes a screenshot of every frame on **both ends** to
  `test/out/rc`.
- `core/crates/bl-node/tests/control_offer.rs` was rewritten to assert the property that matters —
  that an unbidden take-up signal is dropped, that an accept with no offer behind it is refused,
  that an offer is answered once, and that a nudge through a shut door is silence.

## A core test that had been red on main, and why

`bl-node`'s `devices` test was failing before any of this was written, and the reason is worth
keeping: it still counted device-list epochs 2, 3, 4, 5. **0.15.153 changed that rule.** A recovery
file's epoch is where the account stood when the file was written, and the account has usually moved
on since — so one-past-the-file can collide with a list the other devices already hold: equal epoch,
different devices, and no way to tell which is newer. A restore now takes its epoch from the clock
instead, which is past every counter the account has ever used.

The behaviour was right and the test had never been told. It now asserts the rule as it is: the
restore's epoch is past the file's counter and taken from the clock, and every change after it is
exactly one epoch on from that. Named here because a test that has been red for weeks is a test
nobody is reading.

## Still broken, and not fixed by this

Two faults named in `test/e2e-sync.mjs`, which stays red on purpose: **a space still does not reach
a second device of the same account**, and **restoring an account on a phone leaves the app blank**.
Neither is touched by this release.
